outcome: An arXiv preprint (2609.14281, Sept 2026) by independent researcher Patrick White claims to prove that every 4-partite 4-uniform hypergraph with matching number ν(H)=2 satisfies τ(H)≤6, confirming an unpublished 1979 claim of Tuza and closing the case (r,ν)=(4,2) of Ryser's conjecture, improving the prior best bound τ≤7 due to Haxell and Scott (2012). The proof is explicitly stated by the author to have been found through AI-driven reasoning (GPT-5.6 Sol) with independent computational verification (MILP/enumeration) by the human author; it has not yet been digested by any expert, accepted by a journal, or covered in survey/blog literature.

ai.basis_quote: The proof was found through four rounds of structured reasoning with GPT-5.6 Sol (OpenAI, model gpt-5.6-sol-pro) ... Every structural claim returned by the model was independently verified by the author's own exact computation (MILP via scipy.optimize.milp and brute-force enumeration) before incorporation. ... Claude (Anthropic) served throughout in the framing and verification role: building the independent checker infrastructure, posing each round's scoped target, and declining to accept any claim until independently checked.

summary: Ryser's conjecture (τ(H) ≤ (r−1)ν(H) for r-partite r-uniform hypergraphs) remains fully open for r≥4 as a general statement; it is proved only for r≤3 (König for r=2, Aharoni 2001 for r=3). The one concrete development in the window is arXiv:2609.14281 (submitted 2026-09-13), in which independent researcher Patrick White claims to settle the specific case (r,ν)=(4,2): every 4-partite 4-uniform hypergraph with matching number 2 has τ(H)≤6. This is a genuine restriction/case of Ryser's conjecture as stated (not a variant), improving the previous best bound of τ≤7 from Haxell and Scott's 2012 paper (an ε-weakened form of the general r=4 conjecture). Since it settles one case rather than the general r=4 conjecture (which remains open), I classify this as `partial`-in-scope but `claimed` in status: it is a single-author preprint roughly a week old at the time of writing, with no journal acceptance, no digestion by any expert blog (checked for Terence Tao commentary — none found), and explicitly not independently re-verified by the ProofAtlas collaboration page for this exact problem (which states source-attached computations were 'not rerun or independently checked by ProofAtlas' and in fact does not even reference this preprint). I therefore used `status: claimed` rather than `resolved` or `partial`, per §6.1's rule that a case settlement without expert digestion is `claimed`. On AI role: the author's own account states the proof was 'found through four rounds of structured reasoning' with GPT-5.6 Sol, with the human author performing independent computational verification (MILP and brute-force enumeration) of each AI-produced claim before incorporating it, and discovering 'two corrections to the model's intermediate claims' during that verification. Claude is credited only with building verification infrastructure and posing scoped targets — a `none`-type role on its own — but GPT-5.6 Sol is credited with producing the mathematical content (lemmas, the key 'projection lemma', and the overall proof strategy) that the human then checked rather than produced. This matches `generated` under §6.2 ('an AI system produced the proof ... people checked it') rather than `assisted`, though the human's role in independently verifying and correcting the AI's intermediate claims is substantial and could support reading this as closer to a human-AI collaborative discovery process; I flag this as a genuine judgment call. I also checked the August 2025 paper (arXiv:2509.00619, Domic & Gallardo) flagged by triage: it offers unspecified 'new sufficient conditions' under which the conjecture holds, shows no AI acknowledgement in the abstract/metadata I could access, and does not itself resolve any case — it is `progress` at most and does not change my overall status determination since the White preprint is the more decisive, in-scope event. The current live Wikipedia article (last edited 2026-07-29, i.e. before the White preprint) does not yet reflect either paper.
competing_reading: One could argue `resolved`+`partial` is too strong a rejection and this should instead be recorded as `progress` rather than `claimed`, on the theory that an unreviewed single-author preprint using an AI-generated proof, on a topic where machine/human-verified errors are historically common, should not be credited with 'settling' a case until independent expert or community verification occurs (the ProofAtlas page — a live collaboration specifically tracking this exact problem — notably does not yet list or endorse this result). I chose `claimed` over `progress` because the paper's central claim, if correct, does fully settle a stated case (not merely move a bound), and `claimed` exists precisely for this situation (a definite claim, not yet expert-digested) rather than `progress` (which is for bounds or incidents). A different reader might also contest `generated` vs `assisted`: the human performed substantial independent verification and caught the model's errors, which is a stronger human role than a minimal 'checked and accepted' arrangement; but the author's own text is explicit that the mathematical proof content itself — including the pivotal projection lemma — was 'found' and 'discovered' by the model, with the human's role described as verification and framing, matching `generated` as defined.
what_would_settle_it: Independent verification of arXiv:2609.14281 by a hypergraph-matching expert (e.g., Haxell, Scott, Aharoni, or another specialist), a journal acceptance, coverage on ProofAtlas or a research blog, or a second independent proof of the same (r,ν)=(4,2) case. Also, seeing whether a v2 of the preprint appears with corrections or a withdrawal would matter for confidence.

corrections.by: hand correction directed by a human reviewer (Alex Fogelson) and drafted on that instruction by Claude (claude-opus-5-5); not the researching agent and not any automated pass. Judged from this record's own findings; no new sources were opened
corrections.why: SCOPE: `claimed` counted Ryser's conjecture among resolutions, but White's preprint settles one case, (r, nu) = (4, 2), and the record says the conjecture 'remains fully open for r >= 4 as a general statement' and itself calls the result 'partial-in-scope'. A case settled is `partial` under 6.1. The research rules fold 'how much was settled' and 'has an expert checked it' into one field, and the agent read an unreviewed case as `claimed`; that is the pattern this batch of corrections fixes. The claim is a week-old single-author preprint with no independent check, which `partial` does not record; it stays in `summary`.
